newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian call money ends at 8.75-9.75 pct, off highs.
newsitem.headline: Indian call money ends at 8.75-9.75 pct, off highs.

text.p: Indian call money ended Monday at 8.75-9.75 percent, slightly down from opening quotes of 9.75-10.50 and dealers said they expected rates to stabilise below 7.0 percent in the coming days.
They said most of the day's trade was between 9.5 and 10.5 percent.
Call money rates, around 1.0 percent for most of April, have risen in the last two days as bond issues sucked away liquidity.
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) last Wednesday invited bids for 25 billion rupees of 10-year bonds issued by 25 state governments.
The RBI said on Friday it received bids for 53.81 billion rupees, with some bids from outlying centres yet to come in, and the excess bids would be retained in full.
Dealers said sentiment was further affected by the announcement of an auction of five-year federal government bonds worth 30 billion rupees for May 9.
"The market was largely driven by sentiment today," said R. Narayan, dealer at Bank of Nova Scotia. "Rates were lender-driven and were not indicative of the liquidity in the system."

ICICI Securities and Finance Company said in a debt market report it expected call money to trade between 4.0 percent and 7.0 percent through May as liquidity with banks remained good enough to prevent a sustained rise in rates.
Prices of government securities fell in moderate trade on Monday, dealers said.
Higher call money rates led to selling interest, pushing prices down, they said.
Trades were worth 2.60 billion against the weekend's 1.14 billion, they said.

The 13.50 percent government stock 1997 fell to 101.40 rupees against its last traded price of 101.51 rupees, the 13.50 percent 1998 to 102.30 rupees from 102.65 rupees, and the 13.70 percent 1999 stock to 103.65 rupees from 104.10 rupees, dealers said.
They said treasury bills were also actively traded on Monday with the April 1998 maturity bills yielding 9.65 percent against 9.50 percent.
